rows.verified: Employers must assess risks to workers from noise exposure at work.
Employers must reduce noise exposure where it creates health or safety risks.
Technical and organisational noise controls should be considered before relying on hearing protection.
Hearing protection is required where remaining exposure cannot be reduced enough by other methods.
Noise-control equipment and hearing protectors must be maintained and used properly.
Workers exposed above the lower action values need information and training about risks and controls.
Health surveillance is required where workers remain at risk of noise-induced hearing damage.
Noise can also create safety risks by masking communication and warning signals.
Required action depends on measured daily or weekly exposure, peak sound pressure, duration and the actual work pattern.
Occupational-noise guidance is exposure-specific context and is not an exact parcel-level safety probability.
Regular exposure to hand-arm vibration can cause permanent injury to blood vessels, nerves, joints and muscles.
Employers should identify tools, machines and processes that expose workers to hand-arm vibration.
Risk assessment should consider who is exposed, the equipment used and the duration and pattern of exposure.
Alternative processes, equipment or working methods should be considered to eliminate or reduce vibration exposure.
Exposure time can be reduced through work planning, job rotation or other organisational controls where suitable.
Vibrating tools should be selected for suitability, used correctly and maintained in effective condition.
Workers need information and training about vibration risks, symptoms and control measures.
Suitable health surveillance is required for workers who remain at risk.
Manufacturer vibration values alone may not represent exposure in the actual task, tool condition and material.
Vibration evidence is tool-, task- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level probability.
